blocks.text: **The problem.** You have a pile of stones with weights `stones[i]`. Each turn, take the **two heaviest** stones, `x ≤ y`, and smash them together. If `x == y`, both are destroyed. Otherwise the lighter one is destroyed and the heavier one's weight becomes `y − x`. When at most one stone is left, return its weight — or `0` if none is left.

blocks.alt: The stones 2, 7, 4, 1, 8, 1, sorted heaviest first. Smash 8 and 7: 1 is left over. Then 4 and 2 leave 2. Then 2 and 1 leave 1. Then 1 and 1 destroy each other. One stone of weight 1 remains.

blocks.text: Every turn asks the same question — *which two stones are heaviest now?* — and every turn may add a new stone. That's the heap signal: repeatedly take the largest, while values are still being added.
1. Brute force: sort before every turn
**Time O(n² log n), space O(n).** Up to n − 1 turns, each paying for a full sort.
Sort once. The two heaviest are then always at the end. The only work each turn is to put the leftover stone back **in its place** — find the spot with binary search, then insert it.
**Time O(n²), space O(n).** The binary search is fast, but inserting into the middle of an array still moves everything after the spot.
A **max-heap** keeps the heaviest stone on top. Pop twice to get the two heaviest, and push the leftover back — each in O(log n), with no shifting at all.

blocks.alt: The stones 2, 7, 4, 1, 8, 1 as a max-heap: 8 on top, with children 7 and 4. Popping twice hands out 8 and then 7, the two heaviest.

blocks.caption: Each turn pops the two heaviest and pushes back whatever survives.

blocks.text: **Time O(n log n), space O(n).** At most n − 1 turns, each with two pops and one push.

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n² log n) time, O(n) space. Optimal: O(n²) time, O(n) space. Best: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

items: **One stone** — `[1]`: no turns at all; return 1.
**The leftover is the new heaviest** — `[10, 1, 1]`: 10 − 1 = 9, then 9 − 1 = 8.
**Last Stone Weight II** — you may smash **any** two stones. The heap no longer helps: it becomes a subset-sum problem (dynamic programming).
**Take Gifts From the Richest Pile** — each second take the largest pile and leave its square root behind: the same max-heap loop.
**Minimum Cost of Ropes** — always join the two **shortest**: a min-heap. Two lessons ahead.
